summary: Defines experimental extensions to RSVP-TE that protect the ingress (first) router of a traffic-engineered label switched path, for both point-to-point and point-to-multipoint paths. Fast Reroute already protected transit routers; this extends the idea to the head of the path so traffic can keep flowing if that router fails. The procedures are experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: If the first road in a delivery route gets blocked, drivers need a ready-made detour. This gives the very first router a backup plan, like transit routers already had.

questions: how to protect lsp head node
subtitle: Protect the first router of a traffic-engineered path from failures, not just the middle ones.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE fast reroute (FRR) protects transit routers along a Label Switched Path by finding alternate routes around them. However, it leaves the ingress (head) router unprotected. When the ingress fails, the entire LSP must be re-signaled from another router, causing traffic loss and recovery delay.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds an INGRESS_PROTECTION object that the primary ingress sends to a backup ingress, communicating the LSP details and the next hops to protect. The backup ingress pre-establishes backup LSPs to those next hops. When the primary ingress fails, traffic is redirected to the backup ingress via these backup LSPs, which merge back into the primary LSP downstream, achieving local repair.
tldr.outcome: The ingress node now has fast reroute protection comparable to transit nodes. Traffic can be locally repaired in milliseconds instead of waiting for full re-signaling. The RFC proposes two signaling methods (Relay-Message and Proxy-Ingress) and remains experimental pending deployment feedback.

today: RFC 8424 is an Experimental RFC defining ingress fast reroute for RSVP-TE. The specification remains experimental to gather operational data on the two proposed signaling approaches (Relay-Message and Proxy-Ingress) and their performance characteristics. Feedback from deployments will guide the choice of one approach for a future standards-track revision.

sections.title: The Ingress Protection Problem
sections.content:
MPLS traffic-engineered LSPs define explicit paths through the network. RFC 4090 standardized Fast Reroute (FRR) for point-to-point LSPs and RFC 4875 for point-to-multipoint LSPs, protecting transit routers and links via local detours.

The ingress (source) router of an LSP has no protection in those RFCs. When an ingress node fails, the entire end-to-end LSP fails and must be re-signaled from a different ingress node. This causes traffic loss until re-signaling completes.

A typical workaround is to set up a complete secondary LSP from a backup ingress to backup egresses, with BFD monitoring to detect failures. However, this consumes double resources (bandwidth, state), requires complex configuration, and the BFD detection path may fail independently from the ingress, causing false positives.

This RFC extends FRR to protect the ingress node using a backup ingress that pre-establishes partial LSPs to the primary ingress's next hops, achieving local repair in milliseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss's office can fail. Instead of picking a new boss and redoing everything, a deputy at a nearby office can take over and hand the work to the first team leader on the original route.

sections.title: How Ingress Protection Works
sections.content:
Ingress protection involves four elements: setup of backup LSP forwarding state, detection of the primary ingress failure, maintaining the control-plane state during repair, and global repair after detection.

The primary ingress signals the backup ingress via a new INGRESS_PROTECTION object in RSVP-TE PATH messages. This object carries the backup ingress address, descriptions of the traffic to protect (interface indices, IP prefixes, or application IDs), and the next hops and labels from the primary LSP. The backup ingress uses this information to create backup LSPs to those next hops.

When the primary ingress fails, the backup ingress detects it and begins forwarding traffic received from the source into the backup LSP(s), where it merges into the primary LSP at the next hops. The RFC defines two failure-detection modes: Source-Detect (the source node detects failure and switches to backup ingress) and Backup-Source-Detect (both source and backup ingress detect failure quickly).

After the failure is detected and primary ingress is confirmed down, the backup ingress refreshes the PATH messages to the next hops as if it were the primary ingress, maintaining the RSVP-TE state. Finally, either the primary ingress is restored and re-signals the LSP (revertive behavior), or the backup ingress computes a new optimal path and signals a new LSP from itself (global repair).
sections.plainLanguage: The deputy tells the backup driver: here are the team leaders (next hops) and what truck label they use. The backup driver sits by with a truck ready. When the real boss disappears, the backup driver hands the truck to the first team leader, and traffic keeps moving. Later, the boss comes back and takes over again.

sections.title: The INGRESS_PROTECTION Object and Subobjects
sections.content:
The INGRESS_PROTECTION object (Class Number 124-127, Class Type 1) carries signaling information between primary and backup ingress. It includes reserved fields, a Number of Unprotected Branches (NUB) count for P2MP LSPs, flags, and options.

Flags report status: 'Ingress local protection available' (set by backup after backup LSPs are ready), 'Ingress local protection in use' (set when the backup is actively forwarding traffic), and 'Bandwidth protection' (set if backup LSPs guarantee the desired bandwidth).

Options are directives from the primary ingress: 'Revert to Ingress' (indicates traffic should revert when primary is restored) and 'P2MP Backup' (requests a backup P2MP LSP instead of multiple P2P LSPs).

Subobjects include the Backup Ingress IPv4 or IPv6 address, optional Ingress IPv4 or IPv6 address, a TRAFFIC_DESCRIPTOR (Interface, IPv4 Prefix, IPv6 Prefix, or Application Identifier traffic elements), and Label-Routes (next hops and their labels copied from the primary LSP's RECORD_ROUTE objects).
sections.plainLanguage: The deputy's message to the backup driver says: boss is at this address, next hops are at these addresses with these labels, protect this traffic, and tell me when you are ready.

sections.title: Ingress and Backup Ingress Behavior
sections.content:
The primary ingress configures a backup ingress address and optionally a proxy-ingress ID. It must know the direct connection or tunnel to the backup ingress. The RFC defines two signaling approaches.

In the Relay-Message method, the primary ingress selects one PATH message and sends it to the backup ingress with an INGRESS_PROTECTION object containing the TRAFFIC_DESCRIPTOR and Label-Routes. All other PATH messages are sent with an empty INGRESS_PROTECTION object (no TRAFFIC_DESCRIPTOR). The backup ingress stores but does not forward these messages, using them for control-plane state maintenance after a failure.

In the Proxy-Ingress method, the primary ingress inserts itself, then the backup ingress, at the start of the Explicit Route Object (ERO) and uses a Proxy-Ingress-Id in the RECORD_ROUTE Object to avoid loop detection issues. This method allows the backup ingress to see all PATH and RESV messages on the signaling path, simplifying state tracking.

The backup ingress can be 'off path' (not on the primary LSP) or 'on path' (a next hop of the primary ingress). In the off-path case, it acts as a Point of Local Repair (PLR), setting up backup P2P or P2MP LSPs. In the on-path case, it is already a merge point, so it only needs to set up backup LSPs to other next hops and create forwarding entries for traffic injection.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss tells a close colleague (backup) about the team structure. The backup waits quietly, watching the messages go by, ready to step in. If the boss falls ill, the backup steps up and takes the boss's role until the boss recovers or the work is reassigned.

sections.title: Failure Detection and Recovery
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that detecting ingress failure is implementation-specific. However, the backup ingress MUST detect failure (e.g., via IGP reachability checks or BFD) before the PATH message expires at the next hops. Upon confirmation of failure, the backup ingress modifies and forwards the stored PATH messages to the next hops through the backup LSP(s), changing the SENDER_TEMPLATE tunnel sender address to its own address and the RSVP_HOP to its own interface.

Recovery follows two strategies. 'Revert to Primary Ingress' mode (enabled by the 'Revert to Ingress' option) is preferred when the primary ingress is expected to recover. Once it restores, it re-signals the LSP; when successful, traffic switches back to it. The backup ingress stops refreshing the PATH messages after receiving the 'Revert to Ingress' option, allowing the primary to take over.

'Global Repair by Backup Ingress' applies when the primary cannot recover. The backup ingress computes a new optimal path, signals a new LSP from itself using the same tunnel sender address (to share resources) but a different LSP ID, and switches traffic to the new LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: The backup watches for signs the boss is gone. When sure, it takes the team structure and updates the leaders about the new path. Later, if the boss returns, the backup steps back. If the boss cannot return, the backup finds a new route and sends a new work team.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios and Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC remains experimental because two signaling approaches (Relay-Message and Proxy-Ingress) are proposed. Each has trade-offs in control traffic overhead, state management, and code complexity. Deployment experience is expected to guide the choice of a single standard method in a future standards-track revision.

For point-to-point LSPs, the backup ingress establishes one bypass LSP to the primary ingress's single next hop. For point-to-multipoint LSPs, the backup ingress can use either multiple bypass P2P LSPs (one per next hop) or a single bypass P2MP LSP, as selected by the 'P2MP Backup' option.

The NUB field allows the backup ingress to report when it cannot protect all branches of a P2MP LSP, signaling partial protection. Operators can manage multihoming by ensuring multiple backup ingresses are available or by re-configuring the LSP to use a more reachable backup ingress.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a trial. Two methods exist for the deputy and backup to communicate. Real operators will test both and decide which works best. The system works for single paths (point-to-point) or branching paths (point-to-multipoint), with one backup or many.
